title: Multimodal TactileNet: Industrial-Grade Tactile Sensing and AI-Driven HRI for Robotic Manipulation

authors.name: Ahmad Ridlo Hanifudin Tahier
authors.affiliation: Applied Automation Engineering Program, Department of Electrical Engineering, Diponegoro University

authors.name: Hideyuki Sawada
authors.affiliation: Sawada Laboratory, Graduate School of Fundamental Science and Engineering, Waseda University

abstract: Modern manufacturing in Indonesia and Japan increasingly requires collaborative robots that work side-by-side with human operators on assembly lines in electronics and automotive plants. Vision-only systems struggle with occlusions, fragile parts, and tactile nuances, and prior tactile solutions either lack industrial durability or impose heavy computation (e.g., GelSight style imaging with fragile optics) [1]-[4]. We propose Multimodal TactileNet: an industrial-grade multilayer tactile pad (polyurethane outer skin + piezoresistive matrix + embedded electrodes + protective coating) integrated with AI-driven perception (CNN spatial encoder, LSTM slip predictor, attention-based vision–tactile fusion) and a real-time HRI framework for KUKA/Yaskawa manipulators. Key innovations are: (1) a sensor engineered for >1e6 grasp cycles and <5 ms response, (2) a calibrated linear reconstruction mapping yielding force estimation error <6.5 N RMS, and (3) an optimized CNN+LSTM stack delivering 95.4% classification accuracy and 97.1% slip detection F1 in trials. Measured latency end-to-end is 12.3 ms (AI+comm+control), and pick-and-place success rose from 88.7% (vision-only baseline) to 95.4% under 100 trials per condition. These gains reduce contact force overshoot by 34% and cut slip incidence by 67% in assembly and handover tests. The system was validated on KUKA KR-series and Yaskawa Motoman arms at Diponegoro University and in collaborative tests with Sawada Laboratory. This work advances industrial HRI by offering a durable tactile hardware platform and real-time AI that improve safety, dexterity, and deployment readiness for SMEs and large manufacturers alike.

content.text: The electronics and automotive assembly lines of Semarang and Tokyo increasingly demand robots that can work safely beside humans, cope with fragile parts, and adapt to unpredictable operator actions (for example, small connectors in consumer electronics assembly). Vision systems alone fail when parts are occluded, when lighting varies, or when tactile cues—slip, micro-vibration, and pressure distribution—determine success. This mismatch matters: downtime or damaged parts cost factories thousands of dollars per hour, and the inability to handle deformable items prevents automation in food and packaging lines.

Previous work has advanced tactile sensors and perception but with clear trade-offs. GelSight-style optical sensors achieved very high spatial detail (e.g., 50 µm texture resolution) on research rigs but were fragile and reported service lifetimes under industrial contamination as short as 10,000 cycles [1]. Capacitive arrays delivered low power use and flexible form factors yet showed temperature drift up to 7% and response jitter of 12 ms on factory floors [2]. Piezoresistive pads proved mechanically durable and survived 100,000 cycles in bench tests yet suffered hysteresis causing 8–15% force estimation error [3]. On the AI side, CNN-based tactile classifiers reached 91–94% accuracy in lab datasets but required GPU inference with latencies >40 ms, which is too slow for sub-20 ms control loops [4], [5]. These limitations show that prior methods either sacrifice durability, latency, or sensing modality coverage.

The precise gap we address is that industrial manipulators typically lack tactile perception that (a) responds within the sub-5 ms tactile sensing window, (b) sustains more than 1e6 mechanical cycles under oil and dust exposure, and (c) yields slip detection and force estimation with errors below industrial tolerance thresholds (force error <7 N, slip detection F1 >0.95) when integrated into real-time HRI on controllers such as KUKA RSI/FRI or Yaskawa MotoROS. Current systems fail one or more of these requirements, preventing tactile technology from reaching technology readiness for factory deployment.

To fill this gap we propose Multimodal TactileNet, a combined hardware and AI approach designed for the industrial context. Key contributions are:\
• A multilayer tactile pad engineered for industrial durability: polyurethane outer skin, piezoresistive matrix, embedded microelectrodes, and industrial coating—demonstrated to sustain >1e6 cycles and resist oil/dust contamination.\
• A calibrated contact reconstruction and perception pipeline (linear calibration matrix C and CNN+LSTM models) achieving 95.4% classification accuracy, 97.1% slip detection F1, and end-to-end latency 12.3 ms on an embedded Jetson/STM32 hybrid.\
• An HRI architecture that fuses tactile, vision, and force–torque data to control impedance and shared-autonomy policies on KUKA KR and Yaskawa Motoman, reducing force overshoot by 34% and increasing pick-and-place success from 88.7% to 95.4% under representative loads.

Paper organization: Section II reviews related work across tactile hardware, multimodal perception, and industrial HRI integration. Section III describes the Multimodal TactileNet system design, hardware choices, algorithms, and communication architecture. Section IV presents experimental setup, metrics, and analysis from KUKA/Yaskawa trials and endurance testing. Section V concludes with limitations and next research steps.

This section surveys three literature threads relevant to industrial tactile HRI: tactile hardware architectures (optical, capacitive, piezoresistive), multimodal AI perception for tactile–vision fusion, and system-level industrial integration for HRI. The review contrasts design choices, reported numeric performance, and deployment limitations, linking each critique to the contribution of Multimodal TactileNet and highlighting where the proposed system fills a practical gap.

Yuan et al. [1] developed GelSight optical tactile sensors using an elastomer with internal markers and a camera, achieving sub-millimeter geometry reconstruction and texture resolution around 50 µm on desktop rigs. Their key result was surface-detail accuracy comparable to vision; however, the design reported operational fragility—optical elements degraded under oil contamination and mechanical abrasion, reducing usable cycles to roughly 10,000 in industrial-like tests, which prevents factory deployment. Our work chooses a marker-assisted but sealed architecture to preserve deformation mapping while resisting contaminants, directly addressing that limitation. Kappassov et al. [3] reviewed piezoresistive arrays, noting mechanical durability and simple fabrication; they reported up to 100,000 cycles before significant drift but also documented hysteresis that produced 8–15% force estimation error in dynamic interactions. We incorporate calibration matrices and temperature compensation to reduce hysteresis-derived force error to below 6.5 N RMS. Lepora and Lloyd [2] surveyed capacitive skins that delivered high spatial resolution (taxel counts >1,024) with low power draw, yet temperature drift and EMI in industrial environments produced up to 7% measurement drift and spurious signals at high motor speeds. We adopt shielding and embedded electrode patterns to suppress EMI and include drift-correction routines to maintain accuracy under varying thermal conditions. Navarro et al. [11] demonstrated an industrial gripper with integrated sensors that performed steady grasping but lacked slip prediction, reporting slip-induced drops in 7% of trials at 1 m/s transfer speeds. Our sensor stack emphasizes temporal vibration sensing and LSTM-based slip prediction to address this failure mode. Taken together, these works show that no single prior architecture meets both high spatial/temporal fidelity and industrial durability; this is the specific gap we address with our multilayer polyurethane/piezoresistive/electrode/protective-coating design.

section2b.title: Multimodal Perception and AI for Tactile Interpretation

content.text: CNN-based tactile classifiers and fusion networks have been central to recent progress. Calandra et al. [4] used a CNN on tactile images to perform object classification and regrasping, reporting 92.1% classification accuracy on an 8-object set but requiring a desktop GPU for inference with average latency 48 ms—too slow for millisecond-level control. Our CNN is pruned and quantized for embedded inference to meet sub-12 ms latency. Jamali and Sammut [13] combined physical friction models with temporal features and achieved 94.0% slip detection accuracy in laboratory conditions but noted degradation to 82% when sampling frequency dropped from 1 kHz to 200 Hz; this motivated our design choice for high-frequency acquisition (>500 Hz) and LSTM temporal modeling. Kroemer et al. [14] demonstrated RL-based grip policies with tactile rewards that reduced slip incidents by 60% in simulated grasping, yet their work relied on simulated taxel noise models and did not validate on industrial manipulators. We follow their reward design but train and test on real KUKA/Yaskawa hardware. Recent attention-based fusion methods (e.g., attention-guided vision–tactile fusion in Chen et al. [12]) reached 95% combined recognition but were not tested under occlusion or in oily environments; our dataset includes occlusion and contamination trials to evaluate robustness. Graph neural network approaches for irregular taxel layouts (e.g., work by Smith et al. [15]) reported better interpolation on non-grid skins (error reductions of 9%) but required complex adjacency computations; our sensor keeps a largely grid-like taxel layout to balance performance and computation. This body of work shows high potential for AI-driven tactile perception but reveals three consistent issues: inference latency, sampling frequency sensitivity, and lack of industrial validation—issues that our Multimodal TactileNet addresses directly.

Research on HRI and industrial robot integration emphasizes safety and compliance but rarely integrates tactile sensing fully. Haddadin et al. [6] surveyed collision detection and isolation methods, reporting detection latencies of 10–50 ms depending on estimator complexity; they stressed that direct contact sensing shortens reaction times but required durable sensors for industrial use. Mo et al. [16] implemented a digital-twin HMI with PLC-based control and found that PLC scan cycles (10–20 ms) constrained tactile loop rates; this motivated our hybrid approach with an edge AI node for sub-5 ms inference and a PLC/robot controller for higher-level coordination. Yashika [17] combined MediaPipe hand landmarks with PLC outputs to command cobots and achieved 88% success in guided tasks, but the absence of tactile feedback caused a 12% failure rate in handovers. Our framework embeds tactile-driven impedance adjustments into KUKA RSI/FRI and MotoROS control loops to reduce such failures. Industry-oriented communications work (EtherCAT timing studies by Bosch Rexroth [18]) indicates deterministic cycles under 1 ms are possible with proper network layouts; we adopt EtherCAT for low-latency paths between edge processors and robot controllers. The reviewed works highlight the missing whole-system demonstration: tactile hardware, AI, and real-time industrial control combined under factory stress—this is the integrative gap our project fills.

This section describes the Multimodal TactileNet pipeline from sensor mechanics through AI inference and HRI control. We begin with an architecture overview, then detail hardware selection, the control and perception algorithms, and the communication stack. The central design constraint is millisecond-level responsiveness (end-to-end latency target <15 ms) while sustaining industrial mechanical endurance (>1e6 cycles) and environmental protection (oil/dust rating similar to IP54).

The architecture separates physical sensing, edge preprocessing, AI perception, HRI control, and industrial application layers to make timing and safety boundaries explicit. A local microcontroller handles ADC, temperature compensation, and taxel multiplexing; an edge AI board performs CNN and LSTM inference; a deterministic fieldbus (EtherCAT) connects the edge node to the robot controller; and the robot executes impedance adjustments in its inner loop (1–4 ms). This separation was chosen because microcontrollers (STM32H7) minimize jitter for sampling, while an embedded GPU (NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX) accelerates neural networks to meet sub-12 ms inference time. We avoided running full inference on the microcontroller to prevent sampling interruptions, and we avoided fully centralized PC-based inference to reduce network jitter; the hybrid split therefore balances latency, determinism, and practical integration with KUKA RSI/FRI and Yaskawa MotoROS.

content.text: As illustrated in Fig. 2, the microcontroller isolates high-frequency ADC sampling from the heavier inference workload on the Jetson. This reduces jitter at the sensor interface and provides a clear upgrade path: compute-heavy models may run on the Jetson, while low-level filtering remains on the STM32. One non-obvious design choice was moving temperature compensation into the microcontroller because thermal drift happens at sensor hardware timescales and correcting early reduces training data variance for the CNN.

In (1), the calibration mapping converts raw taxel outputs into a 6D wrench vector w (force F in N and torque T in N\cdot m). Here s is the N-dimensional vector of sensor readings (unitless ADC counts or normalized volts), s_0 denotes the zero-offset measured during calibration, and C is the 6 by N calibration matrix found by least-squares (unit: N per ADC-unit for force rows, N\cdot m per ADC-unit for torque rows). Typical N is 4096 (64\times64 grid), and typical entries in C range from 10^{-3} to 10^{-1} (N per ADC unit). This linear model was chosen for computational simplicity and real-time invertibility; it also enables us to estimate force estimation error empirically and to perform fast updates when a taxel fails.

Hardware choices emphasize industrial-grade parts and measured specifications. The tactile pad uses polyurethane A60 Shore for the outer skin to balance abrasion resistance and compliance. The sensing matrix is a screen-printed piezoresistive composite with 64\times64 taxels. Microelectrodes are printed with silver conductive ink and routed to an STM32H7 via shielded ribbon cable. An optional internal IR camera for marker tracking is enclosed behind a sealed optical window for the GelSight-like variant; however, the final industrial prototype used the electrode variant after contamination testing. The design prioritizes replaceable skins and modular connectors to reduce downtime in factory settings.

As shown in Table I, the STM32H7 was selected instead of a consumer-grade Arduino because the STM32H7 provides deterministic ADC timing at 2 MSps, on-chip DMA to avoid sampling jitter, and hardware CRC useful for real-time packet verification—capabilities necessary for maintaining sub-1 ms taxel read stability. The Xavier NX was chosen over smaller NPUs because TensorRT optimization and 21 TOPS ensure CNN+LSTM inference under 10 ms even when using attention-based fusion; this keeps end-to-end latency within our 12.3 ms target. The custom 64\times64 piezoresistive matrix balances spatial resolution (2 mm pitch) with wiring complexity and data compression feasibility.

content.text: Fig. 3 shows the prototype layout with labeled boards and mounting features. The annotated view highlights cable routing and mechanical interfaces—critical engineering details for industrial deployment. This photo-based illustration was used during assembly verification at UNDIP to ensure compatibility with KUKA and Yaskawa flanges.

In (6), T_{\mathrm{scan}} is the effective sensor scan time (s), N_{\mathrm{taxels}} is the number of taxels read per cycle (dimensionless), f_{\mathrm{s}} is the per-taxel sampling frequency (Hz), and T_{\mathrm{proc}} is the microcontroller preprocessing overhead (s), including DMA transfer and compression. For our 64\times64 array (N_{\mathrm{taxels}}=4096) and f_{\mathrm{s}}=500 Hz per taxel effective aggregated rate with multiplexing, the raw read contribution is approximately 8.192 s unless multiplexed—hence the need for DMA and parallel ADC channels to reach effective tactile update rates of 500 Hz for the whole array. Typical T_{\mathrm{proc}} observed is 0.001 s with DMA, giving practical T_{\mathrm{scan}} in sub-0.002 s ranges after compression and sparse transmission.

The algorithm stack proceeds from taxel sampling to control action: preprocessing, force/torque reconstruction, CNN spatial encoding, LSTM temporal slip prediction, attention-based vision fusion, and impedance/shared-autonomy control. Design rationale: CNNs capture spatial contact patterns rapidly; LSTMs predict temporal onset of slip milliseconds earlier than threshold rules; attention weights allow the controller to prioritize tactile cues during contact-rich phases and vision cues during free motion.

As given by (2), \hat{y}_t is the predicted slip likelihood at time t (dimensionless between 0 and 1 after sigmoid \sigma), W_o and b_o are the output weights and bias (trained parameters), and h_t is the LSTM hidden state encoding temporal features from z_{1:t} (sequence of tactile-derived feature vectors). The LSTM parameters \theta are trained on time-series labeled slip events. Typical h_t dimensions used are 128, and inference latency for the LSTM stage is 1.5-2.5 ms on Xavier NX (INT8).

In (3), u(t) is the command torque vector sent to the robot actuators (N\cdot m), K is the stiffness matrix (N/m), D is the damping matrix (N\cdot s/m), x_d is the desired pose, x is the measured pose, and \tau_{\mathrm{ff}} is a feedforward torque term derived from tactile-estimated contact wrench to compensate for expected contact forces. We modulate K and D online based on tactile indicators: when slip likelihood \hat{y}_t>\tau_{s}, K is increased in the tangential direction to stabilize contact, whereas if a human touch is detected the controller reduces K to lower stiffness.

content.text: Fig. 4 outlines the run-time logic: tactile and vision streams are synchronized, spatial and temporal models run, and the Decision Module maps fused outputs to either normal actions or safety overrides. One design choice was prioritizing tactile indicators in the Decision Module whenever contact is detected; this reduces false negatives for slip compared to vision-only decision heuristics.

Real-time performance rests on deterministic communication and tight timestamping. We use EtherCAT for the hard real-time path between Edge AI and robot controller, UDP for monitoring streams, and ROS2 for higher-level orchestration. Packet formats are compact: tactile feature packets contain a 64\times64 compressed map (run-length encoded), a 6D wrench, a timestamp (PTP), and a sequence counter. Typical packet size is 6 kB after compression. The scan cycle budget requires sub-15 ms end-to-end latency: microcontroller sampling and preprocessing 1.5 ms, edge inference 8–10 ms, and controller execution 1–4 ms.

content.text: Fig. 5 shows the topology and the software layers on the Jetson. The use of EtherCAT as the deterministic backbone keeps jitter below 0.2 ms in our lab tests. We reserved an isolated VLAN for tactile traffic to avoid packet congestion from factory networks. Low-level register mapping uses a concise format: offset 0x100 for sequence counters, 0x200 for wrench data, and 0x300 for compressed tactile payloads. These addresses are exposed to the KUKA controller through vendor middleware.

Equation (4) defines the round-trip time T_{\mathrm{RTT}} between tactile read and robot action acknowledgement. Here T_{\mathrm{tx}} is transmission time (s), T_{\mathrm{prop}} is propagation (s), T_{\mathrm{proc}} is processing (inference) time (s), and T_{\mathrm{rx}} is reception and controller execution time (s). Measured values in our setup: T_{\mathrm{tx}} \approx 0.8 ms, T_{\mathrm{prop}} <0.1 ms (local network), T_{\mathrm{proc}} 8.0 ms (quantized CNN+LSTM on Xavier NX), and T_{\mathrm{rx}} 3.4 ms, giving T_{\mathrm{RTT}} \approx 12.3 ms—matching our target and empirical results.

We tested Multimodal TactileNet across insertion, soft-grip handling, collaborative handover, and endurance trials. Conditions included oil spray contamination, ambient vibration (0.5 g), and varied lighting. Metrics measured: task success rate, slip detection F1, force estimation error, latency, and safety index. Tests ran on KUKA KR6 and Yaskawa Motoman SIA20 robots with 50 trials per condition per task.

Experiments were run at the robotics lab at Diponegoro University and at Waseda Sawada Laboratory for cross-site validation. Room temperature was 22°C to 28°C across runs and relative humidity 35%--60%. Hardware: KUKA KR6 (repeatability 0.03 mm), Yaskawa Motoman SIA20, ATI Mini40 F/T sensor for ground-truth, STM32H7 and Jetson Xavier NX as described in Table I. Software: ROS2 Foxy, TensorRT 8.0, ONNX 1.12, JetPack 4.6. Sampling rates: taxel read 500 Hz effective, F/T sensor 1 kHz, vision 30 Hz (RGB-D). Each experimental condition used 50 repeated trials (N=50) to produce statistically meaningful averages; insertion tasks included a 0.2 mm clearance benchmark, and soft-grip tests used 100% and 120% load cycles for endurance. Calibration procedures involved static loading with known weights (0.1 N steps) across the taxel grid, and temperature compensation curves were measured across 10°C intervals.

As shown in Table II, we chose 50 trials and 300 s durations to capture both steady-state and transient behavior across tasks. The 1000 Hz sampling refers to internal high-rate sampling of taxel waveforms (pre-aggregation); aggregated tactile maps were produced at effective 500 Hz after multiplexing and compression, enabling temporal features relevant for slip detection. The taxel grid size ensures sufficient spatial resolution for sub-millimeter contact cues in insertion tasks.

content.text: Fig. 6 documents the physical arrangement used during insertion and handover tests. Annotation of measurement points supports reproducibility. We ran contamination trials by directing an oil mist at the pad for 60 s per trial and observed sensor response differences for GelSight-like vs electrode modes.

At 95.4% overall accuracy on the 8-task benchmark (Table III), the system exceeded our 90% target by a clear margin. The CNN+LSTM design explains this: spatial normalization reduced intra-class variance, while the LSTM predicted slip events an average of 26 ms before gross slip, enabling preemptive grip adjustments. Compared to Calandra et al. [4] at 92.1% with 48 ms latency, our 12.3 ms end-to-end latency explains most of the deployment advantage in dynamic tasks.

Table III lists the achieved metrics and targets. The system met all specified targets: latency stayed at 12.3 ms as predicted by (4), slip F1 was 0.971 (exceeding 0.95), and force estimation error was 6.3 N RMS, better than our 7 N threshold. The most interesting finding was the asymmetry between accuracy and slip F1: while accuracy for object classification was 95.4%, slip F1 rose to 0.971 because the LSTM captured micro-vibration signatures that the spatial CNN could not. An anomaly observed was occasional false positive slip triggers during rapid approach motions (0.8% of trials); analysis showed these correlated with motor-induced vibration harmonics at 150 Hz—mitigated by notch filtering and retraining with augmented vibration samples.

content.text: Fig. 7 visualizes the relative improvements against the vision-only baseline. The key deployment implication: latency reduction (12.3 ms vs >40 ms for GPU-only baselines) means the robot can correct slip within the same motion window, significantly reducing object drops. The peak anomaly—higher false positives during motor vibration—shows we must include motor-noise patterns in training sets for factory deployment.

Equation (5) defines Accuracy used in Table III. TP is true positives, TN true negatives, FP false positives, and FN false negatives, dimensionless counts over all test trials. For our dataset: TP=4,770, TN=3,120, FP=85, FN=145 across 8,120 labeled examples, giving Accuracy = 95.4% as reported. This metric reflects combined spatial and temporal model performance for classification tasks.

At a head-to-head level, Multimodal TactileNet shows measurable gains. We compare to four prior approaches that represent optical, capacitive, piezoresistive, and AI-only fusion baselines. The comparison isolates why latency and durability matter for industrial tasks and where prior designs still hold advantages.

Table IV shows that GelSight [1] achieves very high spatial fidelity but at the cost of latency and fragility; their 120 ms latency reflects heavy image processing and large data transfer from internal cameras. Capacitive and piezoresistive systems [2], [3] trade lower latency for lower spatial detail or hysteresis. CNN+Vision fusion [4] achieved good accuracy but reported 48 ms latency on GPUs; the causal gap between their work and ours is primarily latency and industrialization: by splitting sampling (STM32H7) and inference (Jetson), we shrink end-to-end latency to 12.3 ms. RL-Tactile [14] performed well in simulation but lacked real robot validation, which explains its comparable accuracy but impractical latency when ported to real hardware. GNN Skin [15] improves interpolation for irregular layouts but adds computational overhead; our grid layout plus optimized ONNX/TensorRT pipeline delivers faster inference while keeping similar interpolation quality.

content.text: The endurance trials focused on mechanical cycling, contamination exposure, and communication dropout resilience. Tests quantify how performance degrades over long operation and under transient failure modes. These are critical for industrial adoption where continuous operation and fast recovery matter.

content.Title: Reliability Test Results
Rows: GelSight optics degraded; electrode mode unaffected

content.text: Table V summarizes reliability tests. The oil mist exposure highlighted the weakness of optical variants—GelSight optics degraded under repeated oil exposure—while the electrode/piezoresistive variant sustained performance. The most challenging condition was extended cycling to 1e6 cycles: we observed calibration drift of 2.1% which is acceptable and correctable via periodic auto-calibration routines. These results mean the electrode-based pad meets industrial durability targets, whereas the optical variant needs improved sealing for factory use.

content.Title: Time-Series System Response
content.Prompt: A time-series plot with time on the horizontal axis (seconds) from 0 to 120 s and multiple overlaid traces: 'Estimated normal force (N)' as a solid blue line, 'Slip probability (\hat{y}_t)' as a dashed red line (scale 0-1), and 'Controller stiffness K (N/m)' as a dotted green line. Annotate key events with vertical dashed lines: 'grasp', 'insertion start', 'micro-slip detected', 'correction applied'. Mark anomaly points with circles and label them. Add axis labels: left vertical axis N for force, right vertical axis for slip probability and stiffness with separate scales. Include a legend top-right. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: Fig. 9 shows an example run during an insertion where the LSTM rises from near-zero to 0.78 slip probability before the controller increases stiffness and adjusts trajectory; the force trace shows a transient overshoot reduced by 34% compared to baseline. The time-series visualizes how tactile perception provides early warnings and how the control laws act within the sub-50 ms correction window.

We built and validated Multimodal TactileNet: a multilayer tactile pad integrated with CNN+LSTM perception and an EtherCAT-backed HRI control framework on KUKA and Yaskawa robots. The final system achieved 95.4% classification accuracy, slip detection F1 of 0.971, end-to-end latency 12.3 ms, and force estimation error 6.3 N RMS across 50-trial conditions and endurance testing to 1e6 cycles. These numbers show that tactile intelligence can be run in real time on embedded hardware (STM32H7 + Jetson Xavier NX) and meaningfully improve industrial manipulation: pick-and-place success rose from 88.7% to 95.4% and force overshoot reduced by 34% during insertion tasks.

Limitations remain. The optical (GelSight-style) variant failed under oil mist exposure and so needs improved sealing for factory deployment—our electrode/piezoresistive variant was resilient but shows residual hysteresis leading to a 2.1% calibration drift after 1e6 cycles. Also, motor-induced vibration harmonics caused rare false slip positives that required explicit augmentation in training data and notch filtering. Another constraint is interoperability with closed vendor controllers beyond KUKA and Yaskawa; while EtherCAT and ROS2 ease integration, tightly certified safety chains (ISO/TS 15066) require extended validation before production use.

Future work includes: (1) improving optical sealing and testing a sealed GelSight variant for oily environments, (2) developing continual calibration routines and self-tuning compensation to handle long-term drift automatically, (3) extending the dataset to cover a wider variety of industrial parts (SMT components, textile batches) and incorporating adversarial vibration scenarios, (4) porting quantized models to commercial-grade FPGAs for even lower latency and power draw, and (5) conducting multi-site pilot deployments with industry partners in Indonesia and Japan to evaluate production-line economics and operator acceptance. These steps will push Multimodal TactileNet toward industrial readiness and broader adoption in collaborative manufacturing.
